To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) affordance effects can be dissociated from spatial compatibility effects; (2) affordance effects are not necessarily related to individuals' available affordance; and (3) affordance effects may be restricted to the early stage of action.
(1) affordance effects are not simply spatial compatibility effects, (2) affordance and spatial effects are dissociable, and (3) affordance and compatibility effects are independent.

(a) the affordances of an object can affect the speed of a motor response, even when this response is not the most suitable for interaction, and (b) this effect is independent of spatial compatibility effects, which are present at earlier stages of motor response preparation and execution.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the brain represents the world, and in particular, with the representation of objects and their affordances.
the way in which objects are represented and used to guide actions, and the role of the environment and of the observer's motor system in this process.
the interaction between perception and action.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
affordance effects are not a mere byproduct of spatial compatibility effects, but rather a specific and distinct effect that is independent of them, and can be dissociated from them.
the affordance effect does not rely on the spatial compatibility effect, but that both are present in the same task and that they can be separated using EMG.
spatial compatibility effects occur at an early stage of movement execution, while affordances are processed at a later stage of movement preparation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

affordances are not specific to the body, but are instead general, body-part agnostic, and that they are not specific to a particular action, but instead are more general and can be applied to a variety of actions.
affordances do not directly influence action.
the visual system can be biased towards the hand that is closest to the object, and that this bias is not necessarily linked to the affordances of the object.
The main takeaway from our work is that
affordance and spatial effects can be dissociated by measuring early response components, and that the spatial compatibility effect does not depend on the presence of an affordance.
the motor system does not seem to use affordance information for the selection of a specific motor action, but rather uses it to bias motor preparation in a body-part independent fashion.
affordances and spatial compatibilities are dissociable and can be measured independently using EMG and button presses, respectively.
